Stage 3 · Reading

The regret nobody puts on the form

Eleven studies, one ranking, and a rule about where regret goes that explains the whole list.

⌛📜
1 · Before you read. Which do you think people regret more, looking back over a whole life?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The regret nobody puts on the form

Written for this course, from Roese & Summerville, ‘What we regret most… and why’, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 31(9), 2005, and the work of Gilovich and Medvec on action and inaction. The individuals described are composites.

1In 2005 two psychologists gathered eleven separate studies in which people had been asked to rank their biggest regrets, and combined them. The result was a list. In descending order: education, career, romance, parenting, the self, leisure. What is missing from the top of that list is as interesting as what is on it. Almost nobody wishes they had started a private pension earlier, which surprises the people who commission surveys and nobody else.

2The researchers then explained the ranking with a single idea. Regret concentrates wherever people see the most opportunity. Education comes first not because school is the most important thing that happens to anybody, but because it feels like the most open door: there is always another course, another qualification, another year you could have used. Where a door is genuinely shut, regret is quieter. That is why the list looks the way it does, and it is a more useful finding than the list itself.

3A second pattern comes from earlier work on the difference between doing something and failing to do it. In the short term, people regret their actions — the thing they said, the job they turned down, the message they sent at one in the morning. Over years, the balance reverses, and what people regret is inaction: the course not applied for, the conversation not had, the opportunity they missed out on without recognising it as one at the time, because it looked like a coincidence rather than a choice.

4You can hear the difference in how the two kinds of regret are phrased. A regretted action has edges. A man who turned down a job offer in 2011 can tell you the date, the room and the salary, and he has been explaining it to himself ever since; what he says he regrets is not the refusal but the six months he spent not deciding. A regretted inaction has no edges at all, which is exactly why it lasts: there is no single moment to point at, so it never finishes being thought about.

5The third pattern is slower and harder to put on a form. People wish they had got to grips earlier with what they actually wanted, and they describe ambitions that had not switched but evolved, quietly, while they were busy defending an older version of themselves. If only somebody had told me, they say; and, when pressed, most admit that somebody had.

6Romance sits third on the published list, and it is where the phrasing gets simplest. People wish they had turned to the right person sooner, and made up after the row years earlier than they did. One woman had not spoken to her brother for eleven years, and they made it up in a car park; she wishes it had been a car park in 2014. Nobody says quality time without embarrassment, but it is what they mean, and several call the cost immeasurable — which is the word people reach for once they have counted.

Text A · The list and the reason for it

In 2005 two psychologists gathered eleven separate studies in which people had been asked to rank their biggest regrets, and combined them. The result was a list. In descending order: education, career, romance, parenting, the self, leisure. What is missing from the top of that list is as interesting as what is on it. Almost nobody wishes they had started a private pension earlier, which surprises the people who commission surveys and nobody else. If only I had saved more is a sentence almost no one says without prompting.

The researchers then explained the ranking with a single idea. Regret concentrates wherever people see the most opportunity. Education comes first not because school is the most important thing that happens to anybody, but because it feels like the most open door: there is always another course, another qualification, another year you could have used. Ask people at seventy and they wish they had tried; ask them at thirty and they wish they had said less.

People wish they had got to grips earlier with what they actually wanted, and they describe ambitions that had not switched but evolved, quietly, while they were busy defending an older version of themselves. Romance sits third on the published list, and it is where the phrasing gets simplest. People wish they had turned to the right person sooner, and made up after the row years earlier than they did. Stage 4 · Wish and if only

Three regrets, three tenses

The verb after wish tells the listener whether you are talking about now, about the past, or about somebody who annoys you.

Two rules that catch everybody. Never wish + would about yourself: I wish I would stop is wrong, because you can stop. And never wish + would have for your own past: it is I wish I had started, not I wish I would have started.

1 · Read the explanation.
Wishes and regrets

About now: wish + past simple. The past tense marks the sentence as untrue, exactly as it does in a second conditional. I wish I knew means I do not know. With be, use were for all persons: I wish I were younger.

About the past: wish + past perfect. I wish I had started earlier means I did not start earlier, and nothing can now be done. This is the pattern for regret, and it is the one this lesson is built on.

About somebody else: wish + would. Use it for behaviour that annoys you and that the other person could change: I wish he would stop explaining it. It is not used for things that cannot change (I wish it would be Friday is wrong — say I wish it were Friday), and it is not used about yourself, because you could simply do the thing.

Ability: could and could have. I wish I could help is now; I wish I could have helped is the past.

If only. Same forms, more feeling, and it can stand alone as a whole sentence: If only I had known. It is common at the start of a sentence with a comma-free clause after it.

Other ways of saying it. I should have said something is a regret with blame attached. I regret saying it is formal and looks back; I regret to inform you is formal and looks forward, and the two are not interchangeable.

The commonest errors at this level
  • I wish I would have started — use had started.
  • I wish I would stop smoking — you can stop; use I wish I could stop.
  • I wish I was younger in writing — use were.
  • I wish I knew that yesterday — a past time needs had known.
  • I regret to say it last week — looking back needs regret saying.

Two things to watch

1 — One step back. To talk about now, go one tense back (past simple). To talk about the past, go one further (past perfect). That single move covers most of the system.

2 — Whose behaviour is it? Would is only for somebody else. If the subject of the wish is also the person who could act, use could.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing the tense after wish

The situation: she did not speak to her brother between 2014 and 2025. They have now made up. She is unhappy about the eleven years.

Step 1 — when is the regret? The eleven years are finished, so this is the past.

Step 2 — choose the form. Past regret takes wish + past perfect: she wishes they had made it up sooner.

Step 3 — check it is not somebody else’s behaviour now. It is not: nobody is currently doing anything annoying, so no would.

Step 4 — a stronger version. Replace wish with if only and the sentence can stand on its own: If only they had made it up sooner.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
The verb after wish tells the listener when

Regret about now — wish + past simple: I wish I knew what I wanted (I do not know) · I wish I lived nearer (I do not). With be, were is standard: I wish I were younger.

Regret about the past — wish + past perfect: I wish I had started earlier (I did not).

Annoyance at somebody else’s behaviour — wish + would: I wish he would stop explaining · I wish they would answer my emails. This one is only for other people’s repeated behaviour that you want changed — I wish I would be taller is not English, because you cannot be annoyed at yourself this way.

Inability — wish I could for now, wish I could have for the past: I wish I could help · I wish I could have helped.

Stronger, more formal, and with blame

If only takes exactly the same forms as wish and feels stronger: If only I had known. It often stands alone as a whole sentence, which wish does not.

Regret divides by form, and the two meanings are far apart. I regret saying it (or regret that I said it) is a real regret about the past. I regret to inform you is a formal announcement of bad news, and carries no regret about anything you did. The -ing looks back; the infinitive looks forward to what you are about to say.

Should have + participle adds blame, at yourself or somebody else: I should have said something. Compare I wish I had said something, which is regret without the self-accusation. In speech the difference is audible and it matters.

Errors to watch: I wish I know → I wish I knew · I wish I would be taller → I wish I were taller · I wish I have started earlier → had started · I regret to say it yesterday → I regret saying it · If only I would have known → If only I had known.

1 · Read the model.
Model · four paragraphs

You are twenty-six, in a rented flat with a broken radiator, and you have just been offered a job you are going to think about for six months. I am not going to tell you to take it. I am going to tell you that the six months are the thing that costs you, and not the answer you eventually give.

I wish you had decided in a fortnight. Not because the job was right — you turn it down, and that turns out to be defensible — but because those six months teach you a way of avoiding things that you then use for another four years. If only somebody had said that at the time. Somebody did, in fact: your manager said almost exactly this in a corridor in March, and you decided she was being unkind.

There is one thing I wish you had not done, and it is not a work decision. You have a row with your brother in the autumn and you do not make it up for eleven years, because you both wait for the other one to write first. I wish I could tell you how ordinary the reconciliation turns out to be: a car park, twenty minutes, nothing said about the original argument at all. The cost of the eleven years is genuinely immeasurable and you will spend them believing it is his turn.

I wish you knew now what you get to grips with at thirty-four: that ambitions evolve, and that defending an old version of yourself is not the same as having a plan. But you would not have believed it, and I think you would have been slightly offended, which is why this letter is for me and not for you.
